description: Among a billion still stars, a few things move: asteroids, comets, maybe a hidden world. Their motion is only a whisper between two images. We are building a public web tool that lets anyone hear it: pick a spot in NASA’s SPHEREx infrared sky, blink between two moments, and see what moved. Every detection is checked against JPL’s known asteroids.
summary:
NASA's SPHEREx telescope maps the entire sky in 102 infrared bands, imaging over a billion stars. Hidden among them are objects that move: near-Earth asteroids, comets, and possibly undiscovered distant worlds like a hypothesised Planet X. Finding them matters for planetary defence and for understanding how our Solar System formed, but their motion is often just a few pixels between exposures, buried in data far too large to inspect by eye.

Whispers of Motion makes that motion visible. Our Python pipeline queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx Data Release 1 images, selects two same-detector exposures hours apart, removes the zodiacal background, masks bad pixels, aligns them using WCS astrometry, and applies difference imaging. Static stars cancel, while moving objects appear as red-blue pairs. Each detection is verified with the NASA JPL Small-Body Identification API.

We recovered asteroid 2711 Aleksandrov at 15.8 sigma, moving 84 arcseconds in 3.4 hours, matching JPL's predicted motion within one pixel. Our accessible website lets anyone blink between the frames and watch it move. Next, we will apply machine learning across the full SPHEREx sky to find objects no catalogue has recorded.
details:
The Story Behind It

In 1930, a young astronomer found Pluto by flipping between two photographs of the same sky and noticing one tiny dot that had moved. Almost a century later, NASA’s SPHEREx telescope is photographing the entire sky in 102 infrared colours, again and again, capturing more than a billion stars. Somewhere in that ocean of light, things are still moving: near-Earth asteroids, comets, and perhaps a distant world no one has seen yet, like the hypothesised Planet X.

The problem is scale. A moving object may shift only a few pixels between two images, and the data is far too vast to search by eye. We wanted to bring that old trick, comparing two moments of the sky, into the SPHEREx era, and make it something anyone can do. That became Whispers of Motion.

What We Built

Whispers of Motion is a public web tool and an open Python pipeline. On the website, you can blink between two moments of the same patch of sky, watch an asteroid jump, view the difference image where moving objects light up, and see every known asteroid in the field with its predicted path.

How It Works

Step 1: Find. We ask NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) which SPHEREx Data Release 1 images cover a point in the sky. Our test field, RA 0, Dec 0 on the ecliptic where most asteroids travel, is covered by 223 images.

Step 2: Select. We pick two exposures from the same detector, a few hours apart: long enough for an asteroid to move, short enough to keep it in frame.

Step 3: Clean. We subtract the zodiacal-light model (the glow of dust in our Solar System) and mask bad pixels such as cosmic-ray hits, using the image quality flags.

Step 4: Align. We line up the two images with WCS astrometry, so every star lands on exactly the same pixel.

Step 5: Subtract. Difference imaging cancels the still stars. Anything that moved leaves a pair of spots: red where it was, blue where it went.

Step 6: Verify. We ask the NASA JPL Small-Body Identification API which known asteroids should be in that patch of sky at those exact times, and compare.

What We Found

Asteroid 2711 Aleksandrov, photographed twice on 5 July 2025, 3.4 hours apart.

- Detected at 15.8 and 9.3 sigma (5 sigma counts as a clear detection)
- Travelled 84 arcseconds across the sky
- JPL predicted 14.4 pixels of motion; we measured 13.6 pixels
- Both positions were shifted by the same tiny amount, agreeing within 0.9 pixels: the fingerprint of one real object in motion

That small shift comes from using Earth’s centre as our viewpoint rather than SPHEREx’s exact position in orbit.

Why It Matters

- For science and planetary defence: a clear, reproducible way to find and verify moving objects in SPHEREx data.
- For students and citizen scientists: a chance to explore real NASA data and see, with their own eyes, how discoveries like Pluto were made.
- For everyone: the website is accessible, with read-aloud buttons, written image descriptions for screen readers, keyboard controls, and reduced-motion support.
- For the community: the code is open source, so anyone can point it at any patch of sky.

What Makes It Different

Difference imaging is how professional surveys hunt asteroids. We paired it with a simple blink experience anyone can enjoy, and we check every result against NASA JPL so people can trust what they see. We also show our limits openly instead of overstating what we found.

What We Learned Along the Way

SPHEREx sees each image at a slightly different infrared wavelength, so stars never cancel perfectly; we scale brightness between images and only trust detections confirmed by JPL. A single exposure reaches about magnitude 17 to 18, so the faintest asteroids stay hidden, and we searched the full images for brighter known asteroids to prove the method works. Midway through the hackathon, IRSA reorganised its data collections, so we moved to the official Data Release 1 and added automatic fallback searches. And to be clear: we have not found Planet X. It is our motivation, not our result.

Where We Go Next

- Scan many more SPHEREx fields automatically
- Train a machine-learning model to tell real moving objects apart from noise
- Flag objects no catalogue has recorded
- Stack many images to reach fainter, more distant worlds

The same trick that found Pluto could one day find the next one.

Tools We Used

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib), Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject and Requests, run in Kaggle notebooks; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, hosted on GitHub Pages; FFmpeg and Pillow for the demo videos. All images and results come from real NASA data. AI tools (Claude) assisted with the website and video editing, and AI-written code generated the background music; AI-assisted media are labelled. The voiceover is our own.

Links

Website: https://ssjemey.github.io/whispers-of-motion/
240-second video: https://youtu.be/Z2Y-_F2qoK0

This publication makes use of data products from SPHEREx, a joint project of JPL and Caltech, funded by NASA.
